newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR urges Tanzania to halt expulsions to Burundi.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR urges Tanzania to halt expulsions to Burundi.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR expressed shock on Tuesday at the killing of more than 100 Hutu returnees by Burundian troops last week and appealed to Tanzania to stop expelling refugees to war-torn Burundi.

The agency also said that the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, would visit Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda on February 6-15 to meet regional leaders and discuss the fate of displaced Rwandans in the troubled area.
Some 750,000 Rwandan Hutus in Zaire were forced home late in 1996 by ethnic Tutsi rebels after over two years in exile following 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda.

Tens of thousands of Burundian Hutus were also forced back to their violent country, ruled by an army dominated by minority Tutsis which the U.N. says has massacred hundreds of Hutu returnees in recent months.

In the latest massacre, a Burundian army spokesman said troops shot dead 126 Hutu refugees expelled from Tanzania who tried to escape from a detention center in Burundi on Saturday. The spokesman said seven soldiers had been arrested.
The UNHCR has seen its core protection mandate evaporate in the region following the mass expulsions to Rwanda and Burundi.
The refugee agency said its head of international protection, Dennis McNamara, was in Tanzania to discuss the fate of 220,000 Burundian Hutu refugees still remaining there.
"We are appealing to the Tanzanian government that there should be no expulsions at a time when a return to Burundi is generally not safe," the agency said.
The UNHCR is also trying to reach several hundred thousand Rwandan Hutus who fled deeper into isolated areas of Zaire after the Tutsi rebellion.
Some 120,000 Hutus are camped in the village of Tingi-Tingi, south of the town of Lubutu and 170 km (106 miles) southeast of Kisangani town, the major supply hub for the region.
The UNHCR said the refugees at Tingi-Tingi appeared to be under the control of Hutu extremists, who long sought to prevent a return to Rwanda, now ruled by a mainly Tutsi government.
Another 40,000 refugees are camped out near Shabunda, not accessible by land, the UNHCR said. A UNHCR plane could not land in the area on Monday because the landing strip was too wet.
A UNHCR team flew to Shabunda last week, reaching the refugees after a long walk through the mud and reported: "It is physically impossible to assist them where they are in any way."
The UNHCR said the death rate had stabilised among the Hutus in the region but malnutrition remained a major problem.
